items.title: @SpringBootApplication
items.context: @SpringBootApplication is a convenience annotation combining @SpringBootConfiguration (a @Configuration), @EnableAutoConfiguration and @ComponentScan on the annotated class's package.

questions.prompt: Which three annotations does @SpringBootApplication combine?
questions.explanation: It marks the class as configuration, turns on auto-configuration, and scans for components starting from its own package — which is why the main class usually sits in the root package.

items.title: How auto-configuration works
items.context: Auto-configuration classes are listed in META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports (Boot 3; spring.factories in Boot 2). Each is guarded by conditions such as @ConditionalOnClass and @ConditionalOnMissingBean, so it only applies when the right library is on the classpath and you haven't defined the bean yourself.

questions.prompt: You define your own DataSource bean. What happens to Boot's auto-configured DataSource?
choices: It backs off, because it's guarded by @ConditionalOnMissingBean
Yours is ignored unless you mark it @Primary
Both are created and Spring fails with NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException
questions.explanation: Auto-configuration is designed to step aside: @ConditionalOnMissingBean means 'only if the user hasn't provided one'.

questions.prompt: How do you switch off one specific auto-configuration?
choices: Delete the starter's JAR from the classpath at runtime
questions.explanation: exclude / excludeName on the annotation, or the spring.autoconfigure.exclude property, disable individual auto-configuration classes.

items.title: Starters
items.context: Starters are dependency descriptors that pull in a curated, version-compatible set of libraries. spring-boot-starter-web brings Spring MVC, Jackson and an embedded Tomcat; spring-boot-starter-data-jpa brings Hibernate and Spring Data JPA.

questions.prompt: What does spring-boot-starter-web give you out of the box?
choices: Spring MVC, Jackson JSON binding and an embedded Tomcat
questions.explanation: WebFlux + Netty comes from spring-boot-starter-webflux; security needs its own starter.

items.title: Configuration precedence
items.context: Boot reads configuration from many sources in a defined order. Later/higher sources override earlier ones: command-line arguments beat environment variables, which beat application.properties/yml inside the JAR. Profile-specific files (application-prod.yml) override the default file.

questions.prompt: server.port=8080 is in application.properties, the env var SERVER_PORT=9000 is set, and the app starts with --server.port=7000. Which port is used?
questions.explanation: Command-line arguments have the highest precedence of the three. Environment variables beat the packaged properties file.

items.title: Profiles
items.context: Profiles group configuration and beans per environment. Activate with spring.profiles.active=prod (property, env var or --spring.profiles.active). application-prod.yml is loaded on top of application.yml, and @Profile("prod") limits a bean to that profile.

questions.prompt: With spring.profiles.active=prod, which files are loaded?
questions.explanation: The default file always loads; the profile-specific file layers on top.

items.title: @ConfigurationProperties vs @Value
items.context: @ConfigurationProperties(prefix = "app.mail") binds a whole group of properties to a typed object, supports relaxed binding (app.mail.from-address ↔ APP_MAIL_FROMADDRESS), nested objects and validation with @Validated. @Value("${app.mail.from}") injects one value and supports SpEL.

questions.prompt: You need a dozen related, validated settings with nested lists. The idiomatic choice is:
choices: Environment.getProperty calls scattered through the code
Reading System.getProperty in a static block
questions.explanation: Typed, grouped, relaxed-bound and validatable — @Value is better for one-off values or SpEL.

items.title: Embedded server & executable JAR
items.context: Boot apps run as a self-contained 'fat' JAR: java -jar app.jar starts an embedded Tomcat (default), Jetty or Undertow. Nested JARs are loaded by Boot's JarLauncher. Change the port with server.port (0 = random free port).

questions.prompt: What does server.port=0 do?
choices: Picks a random free port at startup
questions.explanation: Handy for tests and running several instances; the chosen port is published as local.server.port.

items.title: Actuator endpoints
items.context: spring-boot-starter-actuator adds operational endpoints under /actuator: health, info, metrics, env, loggers, beans, mappings… Since Boot 2.5 only health is exposed over HTTP by default; expose others with management.endpoints.web.exposure.include.

questions.prompt: With a fresh Actuator setup, which endpoint is exposed over HTTP by default?
questions.explanation: Everything else must be opted in — and endpoints like env or heapdump should never be public.

questions.prompt: Kubernetes needs separate liveness and readiness checks. Boot provides:
questions.explanation: Liveness = restart me if broken; readiness = stop sending traffic until ready. They're enabled automatically on Kubernetes.

items.title: Startup hooks
items.context: CommandLineRunner and ApplicationRunner beans run once, after the application context has started and before the app is considered ready. ApplicationRunner receives parsed ApplicationArguments; CommandLineRunner gets the raw String[] args.

questions.prompt: When does a CommandLineRunner bean execute?
choices: Only when the app is run from an IDE
Once, after the context has started
questions.explanation: Typical uses: seeding data, warming caches, one-off checks at startup.

items.title: DevTools
items.context: spring-boot-devtools restarts the app automatically when classpath files change, enables LiveReload, and applies dev-friendly defaults (e.g. template caching off). It disables itself when running a fully packaged JAR.

questions.prompt: Is DevTools active when you run java -jar app.jar in production?
choices: Only if the 'dev' profile is active
Yes, and it restarts on every change
No — it switches itself off for a packaged application
questions.explanation: It also should be declared optional / developmentOnly so it isn't shipped.

items.title: Logging defaults
items.context: Boot uses SLF4J with Logback by default (via spring-boot-starter-logging). Levels are set per package: logging.level.org.hibernate.SQL=DEBUG. logging.file.name writes to a file.

questions.prompt: Which logging implementation does a default Boot app use?
questions.explanation: Log4j2 is supported by swapping in spring-boot-starter-log4j2.

items.title: Testing slices
items.context: @SpringBootTest boots the full application context. Slice annotations load only part of it: @WebMvcTest (controllers, MockMvc; mock services with @MockitoBean / @MockBean), @DataJpaTest (JPA repositories, embedded DB, each test rolled back), @JsonTest, @RestClientTest.

questions.prompt: You want to test a REST controller's request mapping and validation quickly, mocking the service layer. Use:
choices: A plain JUnit test calling the controller method
questions.explanation: @WebMvcTest loads only the web layer and wires MockMvc; much faster than the full context.

questions.prompt: By default, what happens to data written in a @DataJpaTest test method?
choices: It's rolled back after each test
It's written to the production database
It's flushed to a CSV file
It's committed and shared between tests
questions.explanation: @DataJpaTest is @Transactional, so each test starts clean.

items.title: Global error handling
items.context: @RestControllerAdvice classes with @ExceptionHandler methods translate exceptions into HTTP responses for all controllers. Boot 3 / Spring 6 support RFC 7807 ProblemDetail responses (spring.mvc.problemdetails.enabled=true).

questions.prompt: Where do you map a custom NotFoundException to a 404 for every controller?
choices: A servlet Filter that parses stack traces
A try/catch in every controller method
questions.explanation: One central place; you can also annotate the exception with @ResponseStatus for simple cases.

items.title: Bean validation
items.context: Add spring-boot-starter-validation and annotate request DTOs (@NotBlank, @Email, @Size). @Valid on a @RequestBody parameter triggers validation; failures raise MethodArgumentNotValidException, which Boot turns into a 400 Bad Request.

questions.prompt: A @Valid @RequestBody DTO fails validation. The default response is:
questions.explanation: Customise the body with an @ExceptionHandler(MethodArgumentNotValidException.class).

items.title: Spring Boot 3 baseline
items.context: Spring Boot 3 requires Java 17+ and moves from Java EE to Jakarta EE 9+, so imports change from javax.persistence / javax.servlet to jakarta.persistence / jakarta.servlet. It also adds native-image support via GraalVM.

questions.prompt: Upgrading to Boot 3, why do imports like javax.persistence.Entity break?
choices: Jakarta EE renamed the packages to jakarta.*
questions.explanation: Search-and-replace javax → jakarta for the EE APIs (not for javax.sql or other JDK packages).

items.title: Graceful shutdown
items.context: With server.shutdown=graceful, the web server stops accepting new requests on shutdown and lets in-flight ones finish, up to spring.lifecycle.timeout-per-shutdown-phase (default 30s).

questions.prompt: What does server.shutdown=graceful change?
choices: In-flight requests may finish before the server stops
questions.explanation: Important behind load balancers and in Kubernetes rolling deploys.

items.title: Containers
items.context: mvn spring-boot:build-image (or gradle bootBuildImage) builds an OCI image with Cloud Native Buildpacks — no Dockerfile needed. Layered JARs split dependencies from application classes so Docker layers cache well.

questions.prompt: Why do layered JARs make Docker builds faster?
choices: Dependencies change rarely, so their layer is cached and only the small app layer is rebuilt
questions.explanation: Order layers from least to most frequently changing.

items.title: Lazy initialization
items.context: spring.main.lazy-initialization=true creates beans only when first needed. Startup gets faster, but configuration errors surface later (at first use instead of at startup) and the first request is slower.

questions.prompt: What's the main risk of turning on global lazy initialization?
choices: Misconfigured beans fail at first use in production instead of at startup
questions.explanation: Fail-fast at startup is lost; many teams only enable it in development.
